report:
**Conclusion: generally, no.** For knee osteoarthritis (OA), arthroscopy—washing out the joint, “cleaning up” cartilage, or debriding tissue—does not provide meaningful lasting improvement in pain or function beyond placebo surgery or non-operative care.

The strongest direct test was a placebo-controlled randomized trial: lavage and debridement performed no better than sham surgery in people with knee OA. This is important because improvement after surgery can reflect placebo effects and natural symptom fluctuation rather than the procedure itself.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259

The 2022 Cochrane review, which pooled randomized evidence in degenerative knee disease (OA and/or degenerative meniscal tears), found little or no clinically important benefit in pain or function compared with placebo or non-surgical care. Surgery can also cause complications; the evidence suggested little or no difference, or a possible small increase, in adverse events.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease

Accordingly, the BMJ Rapid Recommendation makes a strong recommendation *against* arthroscopy for nearly all patients with degenerative knee disease—even those with degenerative meniscal tears, minimal radiographic OA, or sudden non-traumatic symptoms.  
https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982

**Important exception:** this evidence does not mean arthroscopy is never appropriate. A knee that is *truly mechanically locked* (cannot fully straighten because, for example, of a displaced tear or loose body) warrants specialist assessment; this differs from pain, stiffness, clicking, or a feeling of “giving way.” NICE’s evidence review found no clinically important benefit versus sham surgery at three months or two years for OA generally.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/documents/evidence-review-16
